entry.title: Our flyvis layout test (made by us, pre-registered, 10 Oct 2026): does the real wiring layout help a trained fly vision model see which way things move? Not decided: the test did not run, because it needed more memory than our shared machine has. A pre-registered setup check also failed, so no result would have been read. One short simulation of the 45,669-cell model was stopped three times for lack of memory (peak about 3.0 of 3 GiB); the next attempt (planned run 14) needs a leaner simulation loop. We did not retrain the model after shuffling. A model trained on the shuffled wiring might do better, so this asks a narrower question: does this trained model depend on the real layout? A dated note in the sensory part of Does fly wiring help?; no chart, no ledger row.

Catalogue (10 Oct 2026): 128 entries, 3 new, all grade A, each with its own real-versus-shuffled comparison: fly-distill (no difference from shuffled wiring; a random graph did best), flywire-connectome-scz (mushroom-body model on BANC; mixed, 95.3% vs 95.7%, right side only) and brainlab (only activity differs, about 3.7 times the spikes; no task). Their rows join the controls ledger in a later check; the ledger stays at 44 studies.

Correction: Fly With Me's "Is it AI?" class changes from none to whole-network-or-per-synapse (grade B unchanged): at commit 89b130d its server loads 9,978 trained synapses onto 25 descending neurons by default, contrary to a line in its TRAINING.md. 55 of 94 graded projects now have a trained, learning or search-tuned part.

Lead scan (10 Oct 2026): nothing met the bar for a verdict (0 promoted); all 21 verdicts re-checked (13 code unchanged, 8 no code, 0 changed); the "learns to hack" video approximately 61,944 views (YouTube search page, 10 Oct 2026), still U; 56 videos, all available.
New research report of 10 Oct 2026: the flyvis test step by step (install, setup checks, memory), the 3 new entries, tracking and limits.

Which relays carry the turn? Read by firing rate (our own pre-registered test, brain only, 9 Oct 2026): silencing the relays lowered the turn command to about 60-70% of normal, but silencing random active neurons also moved it, so this is not yet specific to the relays. Silencing other active neurons also changed the turn command, so this relay result is not specific to the relay neurons. With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command fell to about 70% (left eye) / 65% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). With the 17 (left eye) / 20 (right eye) relay neurons that excite the turn neuron silenced, the turn command fell to about 65% (left eye) / 60% (right eye) of normal (3 runs per eye). The left eye's normal range is only 1 Hz wide (24-25 Hz) and the random control is one draw per eye. Caveat in the chart: One model (Shiu et al. LIF on FlyWire v783), brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; 'silenced' means the neuron's output synapses were removed; the normal range comes from 3 runs per eye; not a real fly. The chart replaces the 8 Oct disclosure; the 8 Oct sentences stay only with the label "by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)".

New on How it works: What the map leaves out. The model is one fly's wiring map: 138,639 neurons and 15,091,983 connections, run with one simple neuron rule. It leaves out electrical synapses (gap junctions), neuropeptides, learning, the different behaviour of different kinds of neurons (including neurons that do not spike), the differences between flies and over a fly's life, and the nerve cord and body. So it can show what the wiring alone does, not everything a fly's brain does. Eight parts with one number and one source each, checked 9 Oct 2026; linked from "Is it a brain or just a map?" on Is it real?.

Controls ledger (9 Oct 2026): 44 studies, 35 with a wiring null: helps 17, no difference 8, worse 2, mixed 7, not yet scored 1. New: FlyVL (helps by the fixed rules, fair and strong, but a classical motion detector beats both real and rewired wiring). No scoring rule changed.

4 new entries (125): FlyVL (A), Flappy Fly (B), FlyWire Playground (B), Let It Flyppen (C); fly-with-me added commits (grade unchanged, trained-class re-check queued). Gallery: 56 videos, Idor's Spanish explainer added. All 21 verdicts re-checked; the dzuma "learns to hack" video at approximately 54,805 views (YouTube search page, 9 Oct 2026), still U.
Research report of the eleventh check (9 Oct 2026): relays by firing rate with every run, What the map leaves out, the flyvis code read, lead scan, new entries, method and limits.

How strong must the shadow be? (our own pre-registered test, brain only, 8 Oct 2026): We lowered the input to the looming neurons step by step, from 80 to 10 spikes per second each. The turn command appeared from about 30 per second (38% of our strongest input) on both sides; below that the model did not turn. The escape neuron started firing at the same input as the turn command. A second seed agreed. Caveat in the chart: one model, brain only; the input is a rate we set for every LC4/LPLC2 of one eye, not a measured response to a real shadow; not a real fly; no measured real-fly rate found to compare. New chart and share card.

Relays silenced (brain only, 8 Oct 2026): With one relay neuron (PVLP141) silenced, the turn command stayed (by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)). With all 21-23 relay neurons between the looming neurons and the turn neuron silenced, the turn command stayed (by the left/right contrast (8 Oct)). Disclosed beside them: 'stayed' means the pre-registered turn rule still passed; the ratio we used saturates because the near-side turn neuron is always at 0 Hz; with PVLP141 silenced the far-side rate did fall (left 25 to 17 Hz, right 41 to 24 Hz).

The looming body test, now n 6: real map 6 of 6 turned away (left 3 of 3, right 3 of 3), scrambled 0 of 3 body runs (+3 drives identical to the floor); with the escape neuron silenced, the fly still turned away (2 of 2); with only the inside of the map scrambled, the fly turned away in 0 of 6 runs. The 5 Oct floor run repeated exactly. Updated walking chart.

Build your own: brain (Brian2 2.9.0) and body (FlyGym 2.1.0) installed together in one Python 3.12 environment: 1.1 GB on disk, tested 8 Oct 2026, with numpy pinned to 2.3.5; new common error: AttributeError: type object 'numpy.ndarray' has no attribute 'ptp' on import brian2 with numpy 2.5.3, and its fix.

Use in class: a 20-minute plan on the tested beginner path (six steps, one live sugar trial, the control and the looming result shown from our tests, three discussion questions), with browser demos and play.drosophila.io as no-install alternatives.

New verdict: "Can A Conscious Fly Brain Learn how to Hack?" by dzuma (approximately 37,310 views on 8 Oct 2026, read from the video page): no code linked, grade U. All 21 verdicts re-checked; Gorilla Tag approximately 928,414 views, still U.

Controls ledger: 43 studies, 34 with a wiring null (helps 16, no difference 8, worse 2, mixed 7, not yet scored 1). New: Connectocopter (helps, but a hand-written controller ties it) and Synaptera (baselines only by the fixed rules); our looming row has real n 6 and an inside-only arm. The README-only convention (extraction files with results_in_repo_files false) is documented. No scoring rule changed.

121 entries (5 new): Connectocopter (A), Synaptera (B), Fly Brain Tetris (B), fly-jumpshot (C) and the dzuma video claim (U); 48 of 87 graded projects have a trained part; 55 videos (the dzuma claim video added, link only). projects.json and controls.json version 2026-10-08-run10.

Research report of the tenth check (8 Oct 2026): the strength series and relay silencing with every trial, the body completion, the one-environment test, ledger changes, the lead scan, new entries, method and limits.

Where in the wiring is the turn? (our own pre-registered test, brain only, 6 Oct 2026): We turned the scrambled maps up until they were as busy as the real one. They still did not produce the turn: the wiring, not the amount of activity, makes it. Also: Scrambling only the inside of the map kept about -9% of the turn command and 69% of the escape signal. (-9% means none: the far-side command was absent in all 6 trials) and With the escape neuron silenced, the turn command stayed. (expected: no giant fibre to DNa02 connections). Shown with every caveat in the chart: brain only, 7 drives await body runs, n per arm, a faster input checked first. New chart, census diagram and share card.
